blocks.title: Instrument choice
blocks.sub: local-currency debt for a local-currency book

blocks.text: MNT-Halan lends in Egyptian pounds. Funding that book with dollar capital would create a currency mismatch at the scale of its lending, given the pound’s repeated devaluations. Securitisation reduces the mismatch: loans are packaged into rated bonds sold to Egyptian banks and investors, so liabilities are in the same currency as the assets. It also limits dilution: the CEO put the loan book at $650M in November 2023 (Crowdfund Insider, November 2023), funded largely without new equity for each pound lent. Dollar equity funds technology, acquisitions such as Tam Finans in Turkey, and new-market licences. The model depends on conditions specific to Egypt: a domestic securitisation market with willing bank buyers, a regulator that permits non-bank lenders to securitise, and a loan book with enough history to be rated. A founder in a market without these conditions cannot simply copy it.

blocks.text: The 2023 round closed as the pound fell and many foreign investors were leaving Egypt. One plausible explanation for MNT-Halan’s ability to raise is that equity was not funding the loan book, and the book had a performance record investors could diligence; appetite for a rare scaled Egyptian lender probably also mattered. The 2026 listing follows a similar pattern: launched amid low foreign participation on the EGX, with domestic anchors secured first.

blocks.title: Investor selection
blocks.sub: from foreign capital to domestic anchors

blocks.text: The investor base has evolved in sequence: Africa-focused private equity (DPI, Apis) and a Gulf investor (Chimera) for early growth, IFC in 2024, then domestic institutions ahead of listing: Al Ahly Capital, the National Bank of Egypt’s investment arm and the first commercial bank to take equity in the business, and CIB as cornerstone investor. Local banks already fund MNT-Halan through securitisation; as shareholders, they align the investors who know the loan book with the market where its shares will trade. Whether this sequence was planned from the outset or emerged as foreign capital became scarcer is not documented.

Because the EGX offering is fully secondary, the parent, MNT Investments B.V., sells existing shares and receives the proceeds, giving its shareholders a route to liquidity. The parent will then subscribe for up to EGP 4B of new shares in the Egyptian arm at the offer price, and half or more of its proceeds are reported to return to the listed company (Enterprise AM, 1 and 6 October 2026). The listing therefore both returns and recycles capital, and listing in Cairo keeps the equity in the same currency as the loan book and its funders. The offering priced at EGP 24.50 a share, raising EGP 7.84B (about $150M) and valuing the listed Egyptian arm at about $770M, a narrower perimeter than the group’s $1.4B private valuation; shares rose on debut (Tech In Africa, October 2026; Zawya, October 2026).

blocks.title: Dilution management and decline or delay decisions

blocks.text: Ownership figures are not public, but as with M-KOPA, lending at this scale is funded largely through securitisation rather than equity. No refusal of capital is documented; MNT-Halan raised while many peers could not, which is consistent with a structure that kept it financeable through the funding downturn.

why: Mounir Nakhla raised capital through currency crises and built a repeat securitisation programme in Egypt’s domestic debt market to fund his loan book. MNT-Halan also offers a liquidity event, the October 2026 Egyptian Exchange (EGX) listing of a fully secondary 20% stake in its Egyptian arm, and spans both study sectors: Halan began as a ride-hailing and delivery app in Cairo whose fleet became a lending channel after merging with Nakhla’s microfinance business, MNT Investments.
lessons: Match the currency of the liability to that of the asset where a local debt market allows it: securitisation lets MNT-Halan fund EGP loans with EGP debt.
A local debt market is a strategic asset: a repeat securitisation programme gave MNT-Halan funding that was less exposed to venture cycles, though it depends on bank appetite and regulatory approval.
A domestic listing can provide liquidity for a company whose funders and assets are already local.

facts.investors: DPI, Apis, Chimera, IFC, Al Ahly Capital (equity); CIB (securitisation, IPO cornerstone)
facts.routeText: Own the asset, fund it with local-currency securitisation
facts.status: Egyptian arm listed on the EGX, 20 October 2026

entries.text: MNT Investments, microfinance lending built over a decade under Nakhla; Halan launches in 2018 as a ride-hailing and delivery app in Cairo.
Share swap merges MNT Investments and Halan. $120M raised from Development Partners International, Apis Growth Fund II & Lorax Capital Partners, among others.

$400M raised at a valuation of about $1B: about $260M of equity, including about $200M from Abu Dhabi-based Chimera Investments for a stake of roughly 20%, and $140M of securitised bonds across two issuances (Wamda, February 2023). More than $400M securitised over the year in five tranches (Daba Finance, November 2023).
$157.7M growth round, including $40M from IFC. Acquires Tam Finans in Turkey; Halan Microfinance Bank receives a licence in Pakistan.

Securitisations continue (EGP 3.4B, ~$71.4M, in October 2025) (WeeTracker, October 2025). June 2026: first close of a round led by Al Ahly Capital, the investment arm of the National Bank of Egypt, at a $1.4B valuation (Wamda, June 2026). October 2026: a fully secondary 20% stake in the Egyptian arm is sold on the EGX at EGP 24.50 a share, raising EGP 7.84B (about $150M), with CIB as a cornerstone investor; the retail tranche is 43.6 times and the institutional tranche 11.2 times oversubscribed, and trading opens on 20 October (Enterprise AM, October 2026; Tech In Africa, October 2026).
